confounds: Activity differed by label: diagnosed users averaged about 630 posts versus 528 for control users, with medians of about 396 versus 335; diagnosed users also had more words per timeline.
The corpus is imbalanced: 618 diagnosed users versus 5,464 control users, so rare lexical categories have noisier estimates.
Pooled raw-post frequencies can be dominated by prolific users and sometimes obscure or reverse user-level effects.
Lexical matching was heuristic and not manually annotated for Portuguese negation scope, sarcasm, quotation, lyrics, news, advocacy, or third-person reference.
Source-order persistence is not equivalent to calendar persistence because timestamps and equal observation windows were unavailable.
Topic, fandom, identity, demographic, and collection-source differences may explain part of the observed divergence.
Treatment and diagnostic language may be label-proximal or reflect self-report, making it useful for prediction but inappropriate as evidence of causality or clinical diagnosis.

caveats: Pronoun and possessive matching is only a proxy for genuine self-reference and includes object, possessive, quoted, and conversational uses.
The diagnosed group was more active, so user-normalized rates are preferable to pooled post counts.
findings.evidence_summary: Singular self-reference was nearly universal but substantially more frequent per user among diagnosed users. The effect was stable across all four folds; plural self-reference did not show the same pattern.
findings.prompt_guidance: Weight sustained first-person singular usage more than isolated pronouns, and combine it with affective or experiential language.

negative_results: First-person plural was not discriminative: mean within-user post rate was 3.31% for diagnosed versus 3.45% for control.
Absolutist and negation markers were near-universal and weak; token-normalized fold effects changed sign, so they are not robust standalone signals.
Temporal orientation was unstable. For example, future markers were 2.14% versus 2.10% by user-mean rate, but pooled raw-post rates reversed to 1.90% versus 1.97%.
Certainty markers were weak and inconsistent relative to the more stable uncertainty/rumination cluster.
Conversational markers showed style differences overall—more questions but less laughter and exclamation among diagnosed users—yet are too collection- and activity-sensitive for standalone use.

Context contamination was substantial: negative-affect terms co-occurred with third-person/no-self proxies for 55.5% of diagnosed versus 47.4% of control users, and also appeared in jokes, quotations, lyrics, and news.
